math-predict.text: Start with one hundred dollars. After both changes, is the price one hundred, ninety-six, or eighty dollars? Make your prediction before we test it.

math-rise.text: First, the price rises by twenty percent. Twenty percent of one hundred is twenty. Add those twenty dollars, and the new price is one hundred and twenty dollars.

math-fall.text: Now the price falls by twenty percent. But twenty percent of what? The new price: one hundred and twenty dollars. One fifth of that is twenty-four. Subtract twenty-four, and we land at ninety-six dollars.

math-insight.text: The percentages match. Their starting amounts do not. We added twenty dollars, then removed twenty-four. That leaves us four dollars below the start. Always ask: percent of what?

math-practice.text: A bicycle starts at two hundred dollars. Its price rises by ten percent and then falls by ten percent. What is the final price? Choose one of the five prices on screen.

math-practice-answer.text: The second choice is correct. Ten percent of two hundred dollars is twenty dollars. The bicycle now costs two hundred and twenty dollars. Ten percent of this new price is twenty-two dollars. Subtract twenty-two dollars. The final price is one hundred and ninety-eight dollars.

logic-hook.text: Two, four, eight. These numbers fit my hidden rule. What do you think the rule is? You can test it by choosing another set of three numbers.

logic-guess.text: Perhaps each number doubles. So you try three, six, twelve. Yes, that fits. It is tempting to stop here. But this test has not separated your guess from other possible rules.

logic-test.text: Try something that could break your guess. Three, five, nine. These numbers do not double. Yet they still fit my rule. So doubling cannot be the whole story.

logic-practice-answer.text: The red square proves the claim wrong. It is a square of a different colour. The blue square fits the claim, and neither circle tells us anything about squares. One counterexample is enough.
